guide.title: Regola, Rome: Palazzo Farnese, via Giulia and the national churches
guide.intro: Regola is the seventh of Rome's rioni by toponymic code. Roma Capitale's own boundary list for the rione runs from vicolo della Scimia and via dei Banchi Vecchi round by Campo de' Fiori and via dei Giubbonari to piazza delle Cinque Scole and the lungoteveri along the Tiber. Inside that line stand Palazzo Farnese, Palazzo Spada with the Galleria Spada and Borromini's forced-perspective colonnade, and most of via Giulia, which Julius II opened in 1508. Regola also holds a run of national churches, one each built here by the Spanish, English, Swedish, Neapolitan, Bolognese and Sienese communities, a papal prison of 1652, a papal pawn bank, and a crypt furnished with the bones of more than eight thousand people.

sections.heading: The rione's boundary
sections.body:
Roma Capitale gives the rione's boundary as a list of streets rather than a line on the ground: vicolo della Scimia, via delle Carceri, via dei Banchi Vecchi, via del Pellegrino, via dei Cappellari, Campo de' Fiori, via dei Giubbonari, via di Santa Maria del Pianto, piazza delle Cinque Scole, via del Progresso, lungotevere de' Cenci, lungotevere dei Vallati and lungotevere dei Tebaldi. A street named as a limit is evidence of a line, not of what stands on either side of it, so a building addressed on one of them can belong to either neighbour.

Roma Capitale states that Santi Biagio e Carlo ai Catinari was once inside the perimeter of rione Regola but today belongs to rione Sant'Eustachio. Sources disagree about which rione piazza delle Cinque Scole and the Della Porta fountain standing in it belong to. Roma Capitale's boundary description of Rione VII names via dei Giubbonari among the rione's limits and describes it as a shopping street; Salumeria Roscioli stands on it at no. 21.

Via Giulia was opened in 1508 and runs 950 metres from piazza San Vincenzo Pallotti to piazza dell'Oro. Its southern length lies in Regola; its northern length lies in Rione V Ponte. Palazzo Sacchetti, the Oratorio del Gonfalone and the Museo Criminologico stand in Ponte.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a metro station or a bus route for Regola, so none is given here, and neither are walking times or any distance this guide has not taken from a source. Steer by addresses instead.

The anchors first. Palazzo Farnese and the École française de Rome share Piazza Farnese 67; the palace's guided visits are sold only through visite-palazzofarnese.it. Palazzo Spada, the Galleria Spada and Borromini's colonnade are all at Piazza Capo di Ferro 13. Santa Brigida and the Bridgettines' guesthouse are at Piazza Farnese 96. The Fontana del Mascherone stands on via Giulia, and Roma Capitale's file on it names the rione outright.

Via di Monserrato is the spine of the northern half of the rione, and the addresses on it do most of the navigating: Palazzo Incoronati at 152, Santa Maria in Monserrato degli Spagnoli at 115, San Girolamo della Carità at 62/A in Roma Capitale's numbering, San Tommaso di Canterbury and the Venerabile Collegio Inglese at 45, Chez Dédé at 35. On via Giulia, count off Palazzo Falconieri at 1, Off/Off Theatre at 19, Spirito Santo dei Napoletani at 34, the Collegio Ghislieri façade inside the Liceo Virgilio at 38, the Carceri Nuove at 52, the D.O.M Hotel at 131, San Filippo Neri at 134/B, Palazzo Ricci's second front at 146, Palazzo Cisterna at 163 and Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte at 262.

One trap defeats map software as well as visitors. Via Giulia, via dei Giubbonari, via dei Banchi Vecchi, via del Pellegrino and via di Santa Maria del Pianto are all shared with a neighbouring rione along part of their length, so an address on any of them is an address and not a statement about which rione a building stands in. The streets and rises that lie inside the rione, and that this guide uses for orientation, are via di Monserrato, via del Mascherone, via dei Pettinari, via di San Paolo alla Regola, via degli Specchi, via Arenula and Monte de' Cenci.

sections.heading: Tickets, bookings and locked doors
sections.body:
Regola asks for more advance planning than most of central Rome, because several of its best interiors open only by arrangement.

Palazzo Farnese is entered on a guided tour and no other way. The tours run in Italian, French or English; tickets are sold only through the palace's official visits site, from 90 days ahead until 5 days before, a maximum of 8 per transaction, personal, non-refundable and non-transferable unless the flexible ticket is bought. The published slots are: Palazzo Farnese on Monday at 15.00, 16.00 and 17.00 and on Tuesday, Thursday and Friday at 15.00 and 16.00; Palazzo Farnese with the Sotterranei on Monday at 17.00 in Italian, Tuesday at 17.00 in English and Thursday at 17.00 in French; Palazzo Farnese with the École française de Rome on Friday at 17.00. Prices are 15 euro for the palace, 20 euro with the Sotterranei and 22 euro with the École française, free for children up to 6. Visitors present themselves 30 minutes before the slot with the original of the same identity document used at purchase; identity card or passport only, driving licences and photocopies not accepted. There is no cloakroom, and trolleys, luggage and backpacks may not be brought in, though women's handbags may. No photography inside. Groups are a maximum of 33, and 25 for the Tuesday, Thursday and Friday 17.00 visits. The palace is accessible to visitors with disabilities except for the École française de Rome and the Sotterranei, and the Sotterranei are not open to children under 12 or to visitors with motor disabilities.

For the Galleria Spada, Roma Capitale gives last admission at 19.00, closure on Tuesdays, on 25 December and on 1 January except for special openings under MiC programmes, and guided visits to the palace's Piano Nobile, the Sale del Consiglio di Stato, on the first Saturday of the month with booking required. No source states the gallery's opening time, so none is given here. Tickets are sold online at www.tosc.it/artist/galleria-spada; the gallery's phone is 06 6874896 and bookings go through 06 32810.

Three more doors need a telephone. Sant'Eligio degli Orefici opens Monday to Friday from 10.00 to 13.00 on prior booking on 06 6868260. The crypt of Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte, which holds the bones of more than 8,000 people, is open only by appointment with the Associazione Amici del Tevere, on 339 5852777 or 339 7448084. Visits to San Girolamo della Carità are arranged by telephoning 349 5880020. The Stanze di Santa Brigida above the church can still be visited, in Roma Capitale's words, with access arranged through the community. Two things in the rione cannot be entered at all: San Filippo Neri in via Giulia is deconsecrated and is not open to visitors, and the Scuderie di Augusto have been reburied to preserve them.

faq.question: Can you go inside Palazzo Farnese?
faq.answer: Yes, but only on a guided tour booked in advance through the palace's official visits site, in Italian, French or English. Tickets go on sale 90 days ahead and close 5 days before; you arrive 30 minutes early with the same passport or identity card you booked with, and driving licences are not accepted. The palace has housed the Embassy of France since 1874 and, from the following year, the École française de Rome. The Sotterranei, opened to the public on 29 May 2024, are a separate ticket and are not open to children under 12.

faq.question: What is the Borromini perspective, and where is it?
faq.answer: It is a colonnade in the courtyard of Palazzo Spada at Piazza Capo di Ferro 13, reached at the end of the first-floor museum route through the Giardino Segreto. Borromini built it in a single year, between 1652 and 1653, assisted by the Augustinian Giovanni Maria da Bitonto, replacing a painted perspective by Giovanni Battista Magni. The colonnade is 8.82 metres long and is built to read as about 35 metres: the mosaic floor rises, the ceiling drops, and the planes converge on a single vanishing point. The cast of a Roman warrior standing at the colonnade's end is 60 centimetres high and was placed there in 1861 by Prince Clemente Spada; from the entrance it appears life-size.

faq.question: Is the Venerabile Collegio Inglese part of the Vatican?
faq.answer: No. The college stands at via di Monserrato 45, on Italian soil in rione Regola, and a visitor there is under Italian law. It is a pontifical institution, which is not the same thing as a property named in the Lateran Treaty, and it appears in neither of the Treaty's lists. The same is true of Santa Maria in Monserrato degli Spagnoli and San Tommaso di Canterbury on the same street. Nothing in Regola is inside Vatican City.

faq.question: Which churches in Regola can actually be entered?
faq.answer: Santissima Trinità dei Pellegrini keeps the fullest published schedule: Roma Capitale gives Mass Monday to Saturday and on days before feasts at 07.15 and 18.30, and on Sundays and days of obligation at 09.00, at 11.00 as a solemn Mass said as a low Mass in August, and at 18.30, noting that times may change and asking visitors to contact the church on 06 68300486. Santi Giovanni Evangelista e Petronio dei Bolognesi says Mass Monday to Friday at 19.00 and opens an hour before. Sant'Eligio degli Orefici opens Monday to Friday 10.00 to 13.00 on prior booking. San Girolamo della Carità and the crypt of Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte are arranged by telephone. For the rest, no source states opening hours, so none are given here.

faq.question: Is Campo de' Fiori in Regola?
faq.answer: No. Campo de' Fiori is named in Roma Capitale's boundary list as one of the rione's limits, which makes it a boundary of Regola rather than part of it. On Regola's side of that seam stand the Locanda del Gallo, the fifteenth-century property of Vannozza Cattanei whose family arms are still on the vicolo del Gallo front, and the run of palaces along via dei Cappellari and the Monte di Pietà.

faq.question: What is there to see in Regola without a ticket?
faq.answer: Piazza Farnese, paved from 1545, with its two fountains: Roman granite basins moved from piazza San Marco, turned into fountains by Girolamo Rainaldi in 1626, each with a travertine outer basin, an amphora-shaped baluster, a Farnese lily and seven jets. The Fontana del Mascherone on via Giulia, whose antique mask pours the water into a granite thermal basin. The painted front of Palazzo Ricci on piazza de' Ricci, which Roma Capitale attributes to Polidoro da Caravaggio about 1525 with Maturino da Firenze. The façades of Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte, with its winged skeleton and the words Hodie mihi, cras tibi, and of Santa Caterina da Siena, where Romulus, Remus and the she-wolf stand for Siena. And Ponte Garibaldi, which Roma Capitale says joins Regola to Trastevere.

photos.title: Palazzo Farnese
photos.description: The main front of Palazzo Farnese on piazza Farnese, begun in 1514 and completed in 1589, with one of the square's two fountains at the left edge.
photos.author: Myrabella

places.name: Palazzo Farnese
places.summary: The Farnese family's Roman palace, now the French Embassy and the seat of the École française de Rome. Entry is by guided tour only, in Italian, French or English, with tickets sold only through the palace's official visits site from 90 days ahead until 5 days before, a maximum of 8 per transaction, personal, non-refundable and non-transferable unless the flexible ticket is bought. Palazzo Farnese: Monday 15.00, 16.00 and 17.00; Tuesday, Thursday and Friday 15.00 and 16.00. Palazzo Farnese with the Sotterranei: Monday 17.00 in Italian, Tuesday 17.00 in English, Thursday 17.00 in French. Palazzo Farnese with the École française de Rome: Friday 17.00. Tickets are 15 euro, 20 euro with the Sotterranei and 22 euro with the École française; free for children up to 6. Visitors present themselves 30 minutes before their slot with the original of the same identity document used at purchase, identity card or passport only. There is no cloakroom; trolleys, luggage and backpacks may not be brought in, women's handbags may; no photography inside, and phones are kept on silent and not used for calls. Groups are a maximum of 33, and 25 for the Tuesday, Thursday and Friday 17.00 visits. Accessible to visitors with disabilities except the École française de Rome and the Sotterranei, which are also closed to children under 12 and to visitors with motor disabilities. Phone 06 686011.
places.history: Alessandro Farnese, later Paul III, commissioned the palace in 1513. Work began in 1514, was halted by the Sack of Rome in 1527, resumed in 1541 and was completed in 1589, under four architects in sequence: Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, then Michelangelo between 1546 and 1549, then Vignola between 1569 and 1573, then Giacomo della Porta. The Galleria Carracci was painted by the brothers Annibale and Agostino Carracci. The palace's official visits site dates the work 1597–1608 and describes a vault of 20 metres frescoed with subjects from Ovid's Metamorphoses. The palace has housed the Embassy of France since 1874 and, from the following year, the École française de Rome. The Sotterranei opened to the public on 29 May 2024 and hold two black-and-white mosaic pavements, one of sea animals and monsters, one of circus acrobats on horseback, the desultores. Puccini set the second act of Tosca in this palace.

places.name: Galleria Spada
places.address: Piazza Capo di Ferro 13, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A state gallery of four rooms on the first floor of Palazzo Spada, hung as a seventeenth-century quadreria. Last admission 19.00. Closed on Tuesdays, on 25 December and on 1 January, except for special openings under MiC programmes. Guided visits to the palace's Piano Nobile, the Sale del Consiglio di Stato, run on the first Saturday of the month and must be booked in advance. No source states the gallery's opening time, so none is given here. Phone 06 6874896; bookings 06 32810; dms-rm.galleriaspada@cultura.gov.it; online tickets at www.tosc.it/artist/galleria-spada; site galleriaspada.cultura.gov.it. The director is Adriana Capriotti.
places.history: The gallery was founded in 1927, after the Italian State bought the Spada collection and the palace in November 1926 for 14 million lire. It closed during the war. Federico Zeri became director in 1948, recovered the dispersed pictures and reopened the gallery in 1951, arranging four rooms as a seventeenth-century quadreria with the frames touching and the small pictures hung above the large. Room III was designed in 1636–37 by Paolo Maruscelli for Bernardino Spada. The collection holds work by Guido Reni, Guercino, Orazio and Artemisia Gentileschi, Titian, Parmigianino, Jan Brueghel the Elder, Salvator Rosa, Domenichino, Annibale Carracci, Pietro Testa, Niccolò Tornioli, Michelangelo Cerquozzi, Mattia Preti, Giovanni Lanfranco, Pieter van Laer and Francesco Solimena, a Bernini bust of the Laocoön, and Blaeu celestial and terrestrial globes of the early eighteenth century.

places.name: Palazzo Spada
places.address: Piazza Capo di Ferro 13, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The palace that holds the Galleria Spada and Borromini's perspective colonnade, and that has been the seat of the Consiglio di Stato since 1889. Its façade carries statues of Trajan, Pompey, Fabius Maximus, Romulus, Numa Pompilius, Marcellus, Caesar and Augustus, with their deeds set out in eight panels on the top floor. The square in front of it was merged with piazza della Quercia in the early twentieth century by demolishing the block that stood between them.
places.history: Building began in late 1548 for Cardinal Girolamo Recanati Capodiferro (1502–1559), by Bartolomeo Baronino of Casale Monferrato, who worked from 1551 to 1554 on the family's earlier buildings; the palace was largely finished for the Jubilee of 1550. The stuccoes were made by workshops under Giulio Mazzoni and Diego di Fiandra, and Tommaso del Bosco and Leonardo Sormani. Cardinal Bernardino Spada bought the palace in July 1632 and set Borromini to enlarge and rework it over thirty years. The colossal Pompey in the Sala di Pompeo was found in 1552 under the boundary wall between two Roman houses in vicolo dei Leutari.

places.name: Prospettiva del Borromini, Palazzo Spada
places.address: Piazza Capo di Ferro 13, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A colonnade built to deceive the eye, reached at the end of the first-floor museum route through the Giardino Segreto. The colonnade is 8.82 metres long and is built to read as about 35 metres: the mosaic floor rises, the ceiling drops, and the planes converge on a single vanishing point. The cast of a Roman warrior standing at the colonnade's end is 60 centimetres high and was placed there in 1861 by Prince Clemente Spada; from the entrance it appears life-size.
places.history: Borromini built the colonnade in a single year, between 1652 and 1653, assisted by the Augustinian Giovanni Maria da Bitonto. It replaced a painted perspective by Giovanni Battista Magni. A 200-lire coin of 1990 and a 0.60 euro stamp of 2011 both carry it.

places.name: Piazza Farnese
places.summary: The square in front of Palazzo Farnese, paved from 1545, with eight streets and alleys running into it. The buildings on it are Palazzo Farnese, the church of Santa Brigida with its convent, Palazzo Fusconi Pighini, and Palazzo Mandosi Mignanelli at the vicolo de' Venti corner, which takes its name from a family and not from wind.
places.history: The square was used for tournaments, bullfights, popular festivals and the summer floodings that later became an attraction of piazza Navona.

places.name: Le due fontane di piazza Farnese
places.summary: Two matching fountains built around a pair of Roman granite basins. Each has a travertine outer basin, an amphora-shaped baluster, a smaller upper basin and the Farnese heraldic lily, and each throws seven jets.
places.history: The two basins were moved from piazza San Marco, where they had stood since 1466: Paul III took the first, and Cardinal Alessandro Farnese the second some forty years later. Their origin is usually given as the Terme di Caracalla, though it.wikipedia records that the question is not settled. Girolamo Rainaldi turned them into fountains in 1626, after Gregory XV granted the Farnese 40 once of Acqua Paola water by a document dated 1 September 1621. The southern fountain was restored in 1938–39, both in 1992–93, and the southern one again in 2007.

places.name: Via Giulia
places.summary: Via Giulia was opened in 1508 and runs 950 metres from piazza San Vincenzo Pallotti to piazza dell'Oro. Its southern length lies in Regola; its northern length lies in Rione V Ponte. It is paved in sampietrini and was also called the via Magistralis.
places.history: Julius II commissioned the street from Donato Bramante for three stated purposes: a through route over the medieval lane network, a monumental avenue, and a new administrative and banking centre away from the Capitol. The lungotevere embankments built from 1888 cut the street off from the river and left the garden fronts of the Medici-Clarelli, Sacchetti, Varese and Falconieri palaces facing nothing. Demolitions in the Fascist period opened the gap between via della Barchetta and vicolo delle Prigioni, only partly filled afterwards by the Liceo Virgilio. Palazzo Varese, at nos. 14–21 opposite Santa Caterina da Siena, was built in 1616–18 to a design by Carlo Maderno. In 2008 the street kept its 500th anniversary, and churches and palaces along it were restored and opened.

places.name: Fontana del Mascherone
places.summary: A fountain on via Giulia in which an antique mask pours water into an antique granite thermal basin, set in a slightly sunken paved catch-basin, with a marble backing crowned by a metal lily. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's own file on it names the rione: Regola.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina attributes the fountain to Girolamo Rainaldi (1570–1655) and dates it to the second quarter of the seventeenth century, in grey granite, white marble, travertine and metal, originally fed by the acquedotto Paolo. A fountain for Strada Giulia had been assigned by the Congregazione sopra le fonti as early as 1570 and was meant to run on Acqua Vergine, but the work waited on the Acqua Paola channel of 1612. It was built at Farnese expense, as the lily crowning it indicates. It stood free in a small widening that held an open-air theatre in 1660; the wall behind it went up at the end of the nineteenth century. Roma Capitale adds that in 1720, for Marco Antonio Zondadari's appointment as Grand Master of the Order of Malta, the fountain ran wine for three consecutive days.

places.name: Santa Maria in Monserrato degli Spagnoli
places.summary: The national church of Spain in Rome. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The church grew out of two Catalan hospitals, founded in 1354 by Jacoba Ferrandes and in 1363 by Margarida Pauli and merged in 1803; the confraternity under the patronage of Santa Maria di Monserrato was founded by Alexander VI in 1495. The first stone of the church was laid on 13 June 1518 and the design was entrusted to Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, the work continuing under Bernardino Valperga and Francesco da Volterra. The high altar was consecrated in 1594 and the nave vault finished in 1598; the apse vault and a new high altar followed in 1675. The church was restored between 1818 and 1821 and reconsecrated in 1822.

places.name: San Girolamo della Carità
places.summary: A church whose Baroque façade and high altar are by Carlo Rainaldi. Roma Capitale states that visits are arranged by telephoning 349 5880020; the church's own number is 06 6879786. The Cappella Antamoro is Filippo Juvarra's, with a marble San Filippo Neri by Pierre Legros.
places.history: Tradition puts the origin in 382, when Damasus set Jerome to work on the Bible and Jerome was lodged in the domus of the matron Paola, later turned into a church. In 1524 Clement VII gave the complex to the Confraternita della Carità. San Filippo Neri lived in the adjoining convent for over thirty years from 1551 and began there the meetings that became the oratorio; his rooms survive. The church burned in 1631 and was rebuilt. The Cappella Spada of 1654 is by Virgilio Spada, perhaps with Borromini: jasper and marble revetment, and in place of a balustrade two white marble angels holding a jasper eucharistic cloth, the right-hand angel's wooden wings swinging on pivots to let people through.

places.name: Santa Caterina della Rota
places.address: Via San Girolamo della Carità 80, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A church of a single nave with three niches a side, its late-Baroque façade of 1730 carrying the arms of the Chapter of St Peter's in the tympanum. It has been administered since 1929 by the Venerabile Arciconfraternita dei Palafrenieri; the phone, 06 6865407, is answered on Sundays only.
places.history: The church is recorded in the twelfth-century Mirabilia Urbis Romae and in a bull of Urban III as a parish under San Lorenzo in Damaso, originally as Santa Maria in Catenariis. It was restored in the sixteenth century to a design by Ottaviano Mascherino and rededicated to Catherine of Alexandria. Its polychrome coffered wooden ceiling of the sixteenth century was brought here from San Francesco d'Assisi a Ponte Sisto when that church and the Ospizio dei Centopreti were demolished for the lungotevere. The funerary memorial of the engraver Giuseppe Vasi is here.

places.name: San Tommaso di Canterbury
places.summary: The church of the English community in Rome, attached to the Venerabile Collegio Inglese. Its right flank on via di Monserrato has an eclectic Romanesque portal, four round oculi and arched windows above; inside, the plan is a rectangular three-aisled hall on seven columns, with funerary monuments including Thomas Dereham's by Ferdinando Fuga. Phone 06 6865808; www.vecrome.org.
places.history: The church was known in the seventh century as Santissima Trinità degli Scozzesi. After the Jubilees of 1300 and 1350 a hospice was built and the older church attached to it. In 1579 Gregory XIII gave the whole complex to the Jesuits, who turned the hospice into an English college. After heavy damage in the late eighteenth century the church was rebuilt to a design by Pietro Camporese the Younger and finished in the second half of the nineteenth century by Virginio Vespignani.

places.name: Venerabile Collegio Inglese
places.summary: The English seminary in Rome, adjoining its church of San Tommaso di Canterbury, with a summer residence at Rocca di Papa. It is a pontifical institution standing on Italian soil in Regola, and it is named in neither of the Lateran Treaty's lists of properties.
places.history: In 1362 an English merchant couple sold the guild of the English in Rome a house at what is now via di Monserrato 45, and the guild founded there the Ospizio inglese della Santissima Trinità e di San Tommaso. William Allen turned the hospice into a seminary in 1576; the first seminarians arrived in 1577, and Gregory XIII's foundation bull followed in 1579.

places.name: Santa Brigida
places.summary: The Swedish national church, on piazza Farnese, with a late-Baroque façade begun in 1705, two Corinthian columns and statues of Brigida and Catherine above the tympanum; the slender red-brick campanile is late nineteenth century. Phone 06 68892596; www.brigidine.org.
places.history: Birgitta Birgersdotter reached Rome in 1349, and the small church was dedicated to her in 1391, the year after her canonisation. It forms one complex with the hospice she had built and with the house where she and her daughter Catherine of Sweden lived until their deaths. The barrel vault was frescoed in 1709 by Biagio Puccini with the Gloria di santa Brigida, and six canvases of her life are by the same hand. On the right altar is a late-seventeenth-century copy of a lost Annibale Carracci Madonna col Bambino, and the funerary monument to Nils Bielke of 1768 is by Tommaso Righi to designs by Pietro Camporese the Elder. The Bridgettine sisters have held the church again since 1931.

places.name: Stanze di Santa Brigida
places.summary: The saint's rooms are above the church and Roma Capitale states that they can still be visited. Access is arranged with the community; no source states fixed hours.
places.history: The rooms are part of the house in which Birgitta Birgersdotter and her daughter Catherine of Sweden lived, which forms one complex with the church of Santa Brigida on piazza Farnese.

places.name: Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte
places.summary: The church of a confraternity founded in 1538 to give Christian burial to abandoned bodies recovered from the Tiber and the Roman Campagna. Its eighteenth-century façade carries festoons, pilasters, skulls and funerary emblems and two incised plaques, one a winged skeleton with the words Hodie mihi, cras tibi, the other Death seated with a winged hourglass watching a dying man. The crypt is open only by appointment with the Associazione Amici del Tevere, on 339 5852777 or 339 7448084.
places.history: Roma Capitale dates the building to the sixteenth century, while it.wikipedia's article on via Giulia gives 1575–76 and records a demolition in 1733 and a rebuilding in 1737 to a design by Ferdinando Fuga. Inside, under an oval dome, are frescoes by Giovanni Lanfranco of the hermits Antony Abbot, Paul of Thebes and Simeon Stylites, brought from Cardinal Farnese's hermitage, and a high altarpiece of Christ on the cross by Ciro Ferri. The crypt is what remains of the confraternity's cemetery, largely destroyed for the lungotevere in 1886. It was in use until the nineteenth century and took more than 8,000 bodies; bones and skulls are arranged into crosses, sculptures and chandeliers, and some skulls are inscribed with the year, the cause of death and the place of recovery.

places.name: Sant'Eligio degli Orefici
places.summary: The goldsmiths' and silversmiths' church, on a Greek-cross plan under a hemispherical dome with an eight-window lantern. Roma Capitale gives the access as Monday to Friday, 10.00 to 13.00, by prior booking on 06 6868260.
places.history: In 1509 Julius II allowed the Università degli Orafi e degli Argentieri to build their own seat off via Giulia, and they asked Raphael for a small temple to Eligius of Noyon. The first building phase ran from 1516 to 1583, with contributions from Baldassarre Peruzzi and Bastiano da Sangallo; the dome is attributed by some to Peruzzi. A structural collapse in 1601 brought down part of Federico Zuccari's altar of the Magi of 1575, and Flaminio Ponzio restored the church and designed the façade in 1620–21. The frescoes of 1575 are by Matteo da Lecce and Taddeo Zuccari. The floor was replaced in 1864 with marble salvaged from San Paolo fuori le Mura after the fire of 1823, and a silver bust of Sant'Eligio holding relics was given by the Bishop of Noyon in 1628.

places.name: Santa Caterina da Siena in via Giulia
places.summary: The church of the Sienese community in Rome, still held by its arciconfraternita. The façade is in the manner of Borromini, and Romulus, Remus and the she-wolf, the emblem of Siena, flank the central window.
places.history: Sienese merchants and bankers lived along via Giulia from the fifteenth century. Leo X recognised their confraternity in 1519, and in 1526 the church, oratory and clergy house were entrusted to Baldassarre Peruzzi, funded by Sienese nobility including Cardinal Giovanni Piccolomini and the banker Agostino Chigi. Tiber floods ruined the building and it was rebuilt entirely to a design by Paolo Posi between 1766 and 1775, the year the new altar was consecrated. Genga's Resurrezione altarpiece was restored in 2008 for the street's 500th anniversary.

places.name: Spirito Santo dei Napoletani
places.summary: Historically the national church of the Two Sicilies, on via Giulia, with a neo-Renaissance façade of 1853 carrying a carved portal, a rose window and Pietro Gagliardi's Spirito Santo in Gloria.
places.history: The site held Sant'Aurea in strada Iulia with its convent. In 1572 it was given to the Confraternita dello Spirito Santo dei Napoletani, who levelled it and built the new church, dedicated in 1574 to a design by Domenico Fontana or possibly Ottaviano Mascherino. Carlo Fontana reworked it heavily in the early eighteenth century, and Antonio Cipolla rebuilt the façade, the cantoria and the apse in 1853. From 1934 to 1984 the church held the bodies of Francesco II of the Two Sicilies, Queen Maria Sofia and their daughter Maria Cristina Pia, moved in that year to Santa Chiara in Naples. Water damage closed it for thirty years; restoration began in 1980 under the rector Natalino Zagotto with the architect Giuseppe D'Emilio.

places.name: Santi Giovanni Evangelista e Petronio dei Bolognesi
places.summary: The church of the Bolognese community in Rome, on a Greek-cross plan with side chapels and a dome. Mass is said Monday to Friday at 19.00 and the church opens an hour before. Site www.arciconfraternitabolognesi.it.
places.history: The Bolognese in Rome formed a confraternity in 1575, recognised by Gregory XIII in 1576, and built a new church in place of one that had belonged to the Spanish community. Work began in 1582 to a design by Ottaviano Nonni, il Mascherino, and finished only in the mid-seventeenth century; the façade dates from 1696–1700. The church was suppressed in 1810 and used as a warehouse, then restored in 1873 after the confraternity was re-formed. Francesco Gessi's Morte di San Giuseppe hangs on the right altar and Marcantonio Franceschini's double-sided processional painting, made for the canonisation of Catherine of Bologna in 1712, on the left. Domenichino's high altarpiece was requisitioned by Napoleon in 1813 and is now in Palazzo Barberini.

places.name: Santissima Trinità dei Pellegrini
places.summary: The church of the Arciconfraternita dei Pellegrini e dei Convalescenti, with a tall, slightly concave façade by Francesco De Sanctis. Mass is said Monday to Saturday and on days before feasts at 07.15 and 18.30; on Sundays and days of obligation at 09.00, at 11.00, a solemn Mass said as a low Mass in August, and at 18.30. Roma Capitale notes that times may change and asks visitors to contact the church. Phone 06 68300486; 06 68192286 for visits outside opening hours.
places.history: The church stands on the site of the older San Benedetto de Arenula, which Paul IV granted to Filippo Neri and his charity in 1558. The confraternity began rebuilding at the end of the sixteenth century under Martino Longhi the Elder and then, from 1603, Giovanni Paolo Maggi; the church was consecrated in the early seventeenth century. De Sanctis's façade, with its stucco Evangelists, followed about a century later. Antonio Sarti reworked the three chapels on each side in 1853. The church holds Guido Reni's Santissima Trinità of 1625, a marble San Matteo e l'Angelo by Jacob Cobaert and Pompeo Ferrucci, a Madonna col Bambino e santi by Cavalier d'Arpino, and the Auxilium Christianorum fresco brought from the outside wall of Palazzo Capranica.

places.name: Ospizio dei Convalescenti e Pellegrini
places.summary: The pilgrims' and convalescents' hospice attached to Santissima Trinità dei Pellegrini, built in 1625 for that Jubilee and largely demolished in 1940. Roma Capitale records that over roughly two hundred years it took in up to 400,000 people.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that in 1849 the hospice was turned into a military hospital during the fighting with the French army in defence of the Roman Republic, and that it was effectively run by Princess Cristina Trivulzio di Belgiojoso with other Italian patriot women and the American journalist Margaret Fuller Ossoli. More than 1,500 wounded were treated there, among them Goffredo Mameli, who died there at 21.

places.name: San Paolo alla Regola
places.address: Via di San Paolo alla Regola 6, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A church on a Greek-cross plan under a dome with four corner chapels, a rectory of the Third Order Regular of St Francis and the seat of a diaconia. It gives the rione its name.
places.history: Excavations between 1978 and 1982 found stratified walls on four building levels above a Roman street line that survives today; from the age of Augustus the buildings held warehouses and river trades, tent- and sail-making among them. Tradition holds that Paul lodged and wrote here, and a room inside is shown as his. The church is attested from the thirteenth century and was rebuilt at the end of the seventeenth by Giovanni Battista Bergonzoni. A slab of 1096 from the older church survives on the high altar, and there is a fourteenth-century Madonna delle Grazie.

places.name: Santa Maria in Monticelli
places.address: Via di Santa Maria in Monticelli 29, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A church named from a rise in the ground, perhaps rubble, that put it above the Tiber floods. Of the medieval building there survive the three-aisled basilica plan and the Romanesque campanile, together with a fragment of the twelfth-century apse mosaic showing the Face of Christ and a fresco of a holy pontiff in a counter-façade niche.
places.history: The church is first recorded in the life of Paschal II, who restored it in 1101, and was reconsecrated by Innocent II in 1143. The campanile was cut from seven storeys to five under Paul V for stability. Matteo Sassi rebuilt the church entirely in 1716 for Clement XI; Benedict XIII gave it to the Dottrinari, whose curia generalizia it remains, and Francesco Azzurri restored it again in 1860, which produced its present look.

places.name: San Salvatore in Onda
places.summary: A church of three aisles on twelve columns, with a medieval crypt on three small aisles where a large Corinthian capital serves as the altar. Its name comes from the Tiber floods. The Tamburini organ, opus 280 of 1949, has 23 stops, two manuals and pedal.
places.history: The church is of the late eleventh or early twelfth century and is first named in a bull of Honorius II of 1127, which mentions presbiter Crescentius Salvatoris in Unda. Eugene IV gave it to the Conventual Franciscans in 1445, and on 14 August 1844 Gregory XVI gave it to Vincenzo Pallotti for his new society. Luca Carimini reworked it and uncovered the original columns and capitals. Cesare Mariani's Madonna col bambino of 1878 is in the apse, Vincenzo Pallotti's urn is on the high altar, and Elisabetta Sanna is buried here.

places.name: San Salvatore in Campo
places.address: Piazza di San Salvatore in Campo, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A seventeenth-century church now used by the Eritrean Coptic Orthodox community, restored in 2008.
places.history: An earlier church is attested in the first half of the tenth century as S. Salvatoris de domno Campo, from Campo, an abbot of Farfa, and the name appears in a bull of Urban III of 1186. In 1551 that medieval church was the first seat of Filippo Neri's Trinità dei Pellegrini confraternity. It was demolished in the seventeenth century for the Palazzo del Monte di Pietà, and Urban VIII had the present church built on a different site in 1639 by Francesco Peparelli, keeping the name.

places.name: Santa Maria della Quercia
places.summary: The church of Rome's butchers, on a Greek-cross plan with a dome and three chapels, behind a bowed Rococo façade. The emblems of the Università dei Macellari frame the altar image and appear on the metal balustrade, and the butchers still hold an annual feast in front of the church and in piazza Capo di Ferro. Phone 06 6865196; www.confraternitamacellairoma.org.
places.history: The church stands on the site of the medieval San Nicolò de Curte, part of an Orsini courtyard complex. Julius II allowed Viterbesi living in Rome to bring the cult of the Madonna della Quercia here, the oak being also the della Rovere emblem; many of those Viterbesi were butchers, and the butchers' corporation made the church its confraternity seat. It was rebuilt from scratch in the early eighteenth century by Filippo Raguzzini and continued by Domenico Gregorini. Piazza della Quercia was merged with piazza Capo di Ferro in the early twentieth century by demolishing the block between them.

places.name: Santa Maria del Pianto
places.address: Via di Santa Maria de' Calderari 29, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A church left unfinished, with a Greek-cross interior on pilasters and the venerated fifteenth-century Madonna del Pianto fresco on the high altar. Phone 06 6861796.
places.history: In 1546 an image of the Virgin frescoed on a wall of the Portico d'Ottavia was said to have wept at a murder committed in front of it; the fresco was detached and moved to the Santissimo Salvatore de Caccabariis. A confraternity took the name S. Maria del Pianto and began this church in 1612 to a design by Niccolò Sebregondi (1580–1652), leaving it unfinished. The standard with the Miracolo dell'immagine piangente and a Vergine in gloria are by Lazzaro Baldi (1624–1703), whose Madonna e Santi is in the right crossing.

places.name: San Tommaso ai Cenci
places.summary: A church built into Palazzo Cenci on Monte de' Cenci, now a rectory of the parish of Santi Biagio e Carlo ai Catinari. The Roman funerary inscription of Marcus Cincius Theophilus is set between the two doors of the façade, walled there by the Cenci for the name.
places.history: The medieval title was in capite molarum, from the mills on the bank, and the church was also called San Tommaso Fraternitatis as a seat of the Romana Fraternitas; it was renamed from the Cenci palace in the fifteenth century. The interior is rectangular, and the high altar holds a roundel of blue murra, iolite. The first chapel on the left has Storie della Vergine by Girolamo Siciolante da Sermoneta of 1585. The church belonged to the Confraternita dei Vetturini, who had a Mass said each 11 September for Beatrice and Giacomo Cenci.

places.name: Santa Lucia del Gonfalone
places.address: Via dei Banchi Vecchi 12, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A church with a two-order façade and a single nave with three chapels a side, holding a sixteenth-century Madonna del Gonfalone panel and a wooden crucifix over the high altar. The altar was built by Giuseppe Rinaldi about the middle of the nineteenth century and holds a copy of the Salus Populi Romani traditionally given to Livio Agresti. The pipe organ is by Nicola Morettini, 1882. Phone 06 68193368; www.santaluciagonfalone.it.
places.history: The church is attested between the late twelfth and the early thirteenth century and was entrusted in the sixteenth century to the Arciconfraternita del Gonfalone, which restored it in 1511 and 1603. Marco David rebuilt it in late-Baroque form between 1761 and 1764. Its present appearance comes from the complete nineteenth-century rebuilding by Francesco Azzurri under Pius IX, with decoration by Cesare Mariani between 1863 and 1867. The confraternity's own oratory stands in Rione V Ponte.

places.name: San Filippo Neri in via Giulia
places.summary: The church is deconsecrated and is not open to visitors. Its three-bay, two-storey façade by Fiori carries a giant Ionic order and an architrave inscribed DEO.IN.HONOREM.S.PHILIPPI.NERII.DICATUM; inside, the central axis of the three-bay nave is not perpendicular to the façade.
places.history: The church was built for Rutilio Brandi, a glove-maker from San Gimignano who, having gout, had it dedicated to San Trofimo, protector of the gouty; the dedication later shifted to Filippo Neri. In 1797, when the French demanded money from the pope under the Treaty of Tolentino, the church's rector refused to hand over its silver reliquary. Nearly all the buildings around it were demolished from 1938, and the church survived only because the war stopped the works.

places.name: San Giovanni in Ayno
places.summary: An ex-church at the junction of via di Monserrato and piazza de' Ricci. Three explanations of its name are on record and none is settled: Nibby derives it from a founding family, Armellini from a popular corruption of agnus, and Rendina from the Semitic ain, spring.
places.history: The church is first cited in a document of Urban III of 1186 among the daughter churches of San Lorenzo in Damaso, and appears in the Cencio Camerario catalogue as sancto Johanni in Agina. Its parish counted about 40 families and 300 people in 1566, about 60 families in 1660 and about 30 in 1697. The portal architrave records the rebuilding at the expense of Giusto Bonanni of San Gimignano.

places.name: Palazzo Falconieri
places.summary: The seat of the Accademia d'Ungheria, at the Farnese end of via Giulia. Two colossal herms with female busts and falcon heads stand at the ends of the façade, and a three-arched loggia of 1646 with a balustrade of double-faced herms faces the river. The academy holds a library of over 20,000 volumes and runs Hungarian language courses. Roma Capitale gives the opening as Monday to Saturday 9.30 to 19.30; phone 06 68896700.
places.history: it.wikipedia dates the house to about 1515, built for the Ceci family; Roma Capitale dates the building to 1576, under the Odescalchi. The Ceci sold it in 1574 to the Odescalchi, who sold it in 1606 to the Farnese, and in 1638 it went to Orazio Falconieri for 16,000 scudi. Borromini enlarged it between 1646 and 1649, taking the front from eight window-bays to eleven and adding a matching blind portal carrying the Falconieri falcon. Roman river-port remains survive under the building. Napoleon's mother Maria Letizia Ramolino lived here from 1815 to 1818, her half-brother Cardinal Fesch being the resident. The palace was sold to the Medici del Vascello in 1865, altered on the river side in 1890 for the lungotevere, then bought by Vilmos Frankoi and ceded to the Hungarian state in 1927. it.wikipedia gives the Accademia d'Ungheria's foundation as 1927; Roma Capitale says it has been seated in the palace since 1928.

places.name: Palazzo Ricci (Ricci Paracciani)
places.summary: A palace with a painted front on piazza de' Ricci and a second front on via Giulia. The painted front on piazza de' Ricci turns a corner, and Roma Capitale attributes it to Polidoro da Caravaggio, about 1525, with Maturino da Firenze; the ground-floor scenes are the Storia di Muzio Scevola. A stucco canopy at the via di Sant'Aurea corner shelters a seventeenth-century Madonna dell'Orazione. Roma Capitale gives the addresses as Via Giulia 146 and Piazza de' Ricci 132–140.
places.history: The palace was built in the early sixteenth century for the Calcagni, Tuscan nobles in Rome from the late fifteenth century. The Del Bene sold it in 1533 to Fabio Arcella, and in 1542 it passed to Luigi Gaddi and then to Costanza Farnese, who lived there and enlarged it; on her death in 1545 it went to her son Cardinal Guido Ascanio Sforza. Giulio Ricci bought it in 1577, moving here from Palazzo Sacchetti on the same street, and the via Giulia and vicolo di S. Aurea façades were built in 1634. Luigi Fontana's late-nineteenth-century repainting was removed in recent restorations except on the attic. Mario Praz lived here, and Monsignor Della Casa wrote the Galateo here about 1555.

places.name: Palazzo Fusconi Pighini (Palazzo del Gallo di Roccagiovine)
places.summary: A palace on piazza Farnese, still lived in by the descendants of the Del Gallo di Roccagiovine. Its portal is certainly Baldassarre Peruzzi's, though the building was long attributed to Vignola.
places.history: The palace was built about 1524 by Baldassarre Peruzzi for Francesco Fusconi of Norcia, papal physician to Clement VII and Paul III. About 1554 it was inherited by Adriano Fusconi, bishop of Aquino, and passed then to the Pighini. Alessandro Pighini enlarged it in the early eighteenth century to a design by Alessandro Specchi. The Pighini kept an antiquities collection here, including a Meleager with the boar, a Roman copy after Skopas, now in the Museo Pio Clementino. The palace passed to the Curti Lepri and then by dowry to the Del Gallo di Roccagiovine, and Giulia Bonaparte's literary salon met here.

places.name: Palazzo dell'Ordine Teutonico
places.summary: A Baroque palace at the vicolo dei Venti corner. Via del Mascherone separates it from Palazzo Farnese. It has a rusticated arched Baroque portal with its original bossed wooden doors, an image of the Virgin above the portal where the Teutonic Order's arms stood until the eighteenth century, fourteen windows on the two upper floors, stucco-framed on the first, and a rusticated quoin at the vicolo dei Venti corner with a second Virgin at first-floor level.
places.history: The palace appears in Giuseppe Vasi's engraving of piazza Farnese of 1748.

places.name: Palazzo Cenci and Palazzetto Cenci
places.summary: The Cenci family complex on Monte de' Cenci, with a plain flat-rusticated façade and a wide architraved portal, a courtyard with an Ionic loggia and sixteenth-century room decoration. A medieval arch links it to the Palazzetto Cenci, designed by Martino Longhi the Elder. Roma Capitale states that the palace is closed to the public and can be seen only from the outside.
places.history: Most of the medieval palace was demolished and the present building dates from 1570. In the late Middle Ages the area was called Campus Iudaeorum and housed many Roman Jews who moved here from Trastevere after the fire of 1268 destroyed the old synagogue. Roma Capitale records that Beatrice Cenci, accused with her brothers and her stepmother of her father's murder, was beheaded at Ponte Sant'Angelo in 1599.

places.name: Palazzo del Monte di Pietà and the Arco del Monte
places.address: Piazza del Monte di Pietà 32, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The seat of the papal pawn bank, built and rebuilt between 1588 and 1740 by a sequence of architects: il Mascherino in 1588, Maderno with Borromini as collaborator in 1630, Breccioli in 1637, Peparelli in 1639, De Rossi in 1680 and Salvi in 1740. It is owned today by Credito su Pegno S.p.A.
places.history: Paul III approved the founding congregation in 1539, and Carlo Borromeo wrote its first rules. The Monte's first seat was at Banchi Vecchi; in 1585 Sixtus V bought it a building at the Coronari, which gave the vicolo and piazza di Monte Vecchio their names, and it moved here afterwards. From 1584 Gregory XIII made it the deposit bank for civil judgements and for the property of wards and widows. From 1611 Paul V allowed it to lend on agricultural security up to 2,000 scudi. Its cedole were declared payable to bearer from 1724 and circulated as a kind of paper money, and from 1749 it ran the papal mint. It had about a hundred staff in 1835, and the charitable function was split off with the Cassa di Risparmio di Roma in 1836. A Swiss detachment guarded it, and small pledges of up to 4 scudi were taken through rigattieri around the city.

places.name: Palazzo Barberini ai Giubbonari (Casa Grande Barberini)
places.address: Via dell'Arco del Monte 99, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The Barberini family's first Roman house, with frontage on via dei Giubbonari and piazza del Monte di Pietà. It is owned today by the Comune di Roma and houses schools, among them the Liceo Vittoria Colonna.
places.history: The house was assembled between 1581 and 1658 over four generations by buying up neighbouring properties, beginning with a house with four ground-floor shops bought from the Scapucci family on 15 June 1581 by Monsignor Francesco Barberini (1528–1600). It remained the residence of Taddeo Barberini, Prince of Palestrina, until his flight to France, and Barberini property until the 1730s, when the family sold it to the Discalced Carmelites for their curia; it passed later to the Monte di Pietà.

places.name: Palazzo Santacroce (Pasolini dall'Onda)
places.summary: A palace of three storeys with a mezzanine between the first and second, standing between piazza Benedetto Cairoli, via degli Specchi and vicolo de' Catinari. Three of its façades are decorated and the fourth, on the narrow vicolo dei Catinari, is plain; all were restored in the nineteenth century.
places.history: Onofrio Santacroce commissioned the palace in the late sixteenth century. Carlo Maderno drew the design; Francesco Peparelli took the work up between 1630 and 1640; about 1670 Giovanni Antonio De Rossi unified the family's houses into a single body with a loggia.

places.name: Palazzo Cisterna
places.summary: A palace on via Giulia with painted coffered ceilings and walls frescoed with grotesques that incorporate Roman fragments. A Roman cistern survives in the basement that was once the stable. The Fondazione Paolo Francesco e Annamaria Ducci has been based here since 1998.
places.history: The sculptor Guglielmo Della Porta commissioned and designed the palace in the second half of the sixteenth century and lived in it until his death in 1577. The painter Eugenio Cisterna bought it in 1909, decorated its interiors and lived there; after his death part of it was acquired by the Ducci family, who still own it.

places.name: Palazzo Incoronati (Incoronati de Planca)
places.summary: A Mannerist palace on via di Monserrato, built in the early sixteenth century for the Incoronati de Planca, a family from the Kingdom of Spain settled in Rome from the previous century.
places.history: The palace passed in 1569 to G. B. Doni, a cleric of the papal court, and then to the Sacripante and the Luparini.

places.name: Palazzo Alibrandi Cavalieri
places.address: Piazza del Monte di Pietà, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A palazzetto at the via degli Specchi corner, also fronting via dei Pompieri. A wide portal under a family shield carries a first-floor balcony and is flanked by shops and mezzanine windows; above the mezzanine are two floors and a storey added in the 1930s.
places.history: The building was Alibrandi property and was sold to the Cavalieri in the early nineteenth century. It appears in Giuseppe Vasi's engraving of the piazza del Monte of 1759 and on the Nolli map.

places.name: Palazzo Piacentini (Ministero della Giustizia)
places.summary: The Ministry of Justice, in a late-fifteenth-century Renaissance classicism with diamond-point rustication. It is not the Palazzo Piacentini on via Veneto, which is a different building.
places.history: Pio Piacentini designed the building in 1913 for the then Ministero di Giustizia e Culti. Excavation and foundations began in 1914 and were halted by the First World War; the ministry moved in from Palazzo Firenze in 1920, the building was finished in 1924, and the rear wing was raised in 1932.

places.name: Carceri Nuove
places.summary: A papal prison of the seventeenth century, in two blocks: the offices and parlours on via Giulia and the cells towards the Tiber, joined by a gallery open onto the side courtyards. It is now the seat of the Direzione nazionale antimafia e antiterrorismo.
places.history: The prison was built between 1652 and 1655 for Innocent X by Antonio Del Grande, to a detailed programme by Virgilio Spada, replacing Tor di Nona in Ponte, Corte Savella in Regola and the Borgo prison. Innocent X's stated motive was formed when, as Auditor of the Sacra Rota, he saw conditions at Tor di Nona. Before it opened it was used during the plague of 1656 as a stufa where people who had finished quarantine at San Pancrazio and Sant'Eusebio were washed. Prisoners were attended by the archconfraternities of San Giovanni della Pigna, the Assunta al Gesù and San Girolamo della Carità. Until Leo XII there were rooms for clergy, who were afterwards held in Castel Sant'Angelo. A ground-floor kitchen was built in 1824 and the women's prison extended to the second floor; in 1842 the prison held 600 men and 80 women. From 1931 it housed the Centro di studi penitenziari and the Museo Criminologico. It stayed in service until Regina Coeli was built in the early twentieth century.

places.name: Collegio Ghislieri façade, Liceo Classico Virgilio
places.summary: The via Giulia façade of a demolished college, absorbed into the school built on its site. The Liceo Classico Virgilio was built there between 1936 and 1939 to a design by Marcello Piacentini.
places.history: Giuseppe Ghislieri founded the college in 1656 to house 24 sons of decayed papal nobility free of charge during their studies, under the protection of the Salviati dukes. It moved to via Giulia in 1670 and closed in 1928. The building, possibly by Carlo Maderno, was demolished in the 1930s, and its via Giulia façade and some of its decoration survive.

places.name: Locanda del Gallo (Albergo della Vacca)
places.summary: A building at the corner of vicolo del Gallo and via dei Cappellari that was acquired in the fifteenth century by Vannozza Cattanei, mother of Lucrezia, Cesare, Giovanni and Goffredo Borgia. Her family arms are still on the vicolo del Gallo front, and there is a Madonna dell'Immacolata at the via dei Cappellari corner.
places.history: The building was an inn known as the Albergo della Vacca and later as the Locanda del Gallo.

places.name: École française de Rome
places.summary: The French school of Rome, housed in Palazzo Farnese since 1875, with its library on the palace's second and third floors. The library can be seen on the Friday 17.00 Palazzo Farnese and École française tour, which costs 22 euro; that tour is not accessible to visitors with disabilities.
places.history: The institution has occupied these floors of Palazzo Farnese since 1875, the year after the palace became the seat of the French Embassy.

places.name: Scuderie di Augusto
places.summary: A Roman stable complex found under largo Lorenzo Perosi, at the corner of via Giulia and via della Moretta. The excavation has been reburied to preserve it and the site cannot be visited.
places.history: The remains were found in 2009 during the archaeological investigation that preceded authorisation for a 366-space underground car park. Parallel walls and travertine pier bases identify the naves of the stabula of the Circus Flaminius, of the Augustan period and Agrippa's, who was charged with organising the Ludi Saeculares; the buildings were in use to at least the fourth century. A museum display was accepted by the Soprintendenza in 2011 and shelved in 2014 for lack of funds, and the excavation was reburied under more than 7,000 square metres of sampietrini. An opinion of the Consiglio di Stato of September 2018 cleared the way for a garden above the car park.

places.name: Via di Monserrato
places.summary: The spine of the northern half of the rione. Eight streets and alleys run into Piazza Farnese, and via di Monserrato is one of them. Along it stand Palazzo Incoronati at 152, Santa Maria in Monserrato degli Spagnoli at 115, San Tommaso di Canterbury and the Venerabile Collegio Inglese at 45, and Chez Dédé at 35.
places.history: The street carries the name of the Spanish national church built on it, Santa Maria in Monserrato degli Spagnoli, whose first stone was laid on 13 June 1518.

places.name: Piazza Benedetto Cairoli
places.summary: A square at the via Arenula end of the rione, enlarged repeatedly and above all when via Arenula was opened at the end of the nineteenth century. Roma Capitale states that the church of Santi Biagio e Carlo ai Catinari, which stands on the square, was once inside the perimeter of rione Regola but today belongs to rione Sant'Eustachio, and this guide does not write it.
places.history: The square was formerly also called Tagliacozza, from houses belonging to Isabella Orsini, lady of Tagliacozzo. It is dedicated to Benedetto Cairoli (1825–1889), who fought at the Cinque Giornate di Milano and at Custoza, Varese, Calatafimi and Mentana, was Garibaldi's aide in the Spedizione dei Mille, was deputy for Pavia for thirty years, and was afterwards President of the Council and minister of foreign affairs and of agriculture. Roma Capitale's page on the rione records that he lived at no. 113 of the square later named for him.

places.name: Monumento a Federico Seismit-Doda
places.summary: A bronze monument on piazza Benedetto Cairoli by Eugenio Maccagnani.
places.history: The bronze was made in 1905–06 and placed here in 1919.

places.name: Ponte Garibaldi
places.summary: A bridge of two segmental arches, 121 metres by 23. Roma Capitale states that it joins the rione Regola to Trastevere.
places.history: The bridge was built between 1884 and 1888 to a design by the architect Vescovali. Giulio Krall restored it between 1953 and 1956, widening the two original metal spans and rebuilding them in reinforced concrete, which gave the present two segmental arches. The Renella beach and its bathing establishments stood on the left bank.

places.name: Roscioli Caffè Pasticceria
places.summary: A café and pastry shop on piazza Benedetto Cairoli. Its own site gives the hours as Monday to Saturday 7.00 to 18.00 and Sunday 8.00 to 18.00, and states that the indoor room can be booked. Phone +39 06 89165330; info@rosciolicaffe.com.
places.history: No source states the history of the business, so none is given here.

places.name: Salumeria Roscioli
places.summary: A delicatessen on via dei Giubbonari, with its own site at salumeriaroscioli.com. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states the history of the business, so none is given here.

places.name: Per Me Giulio Terrinoni
places.summary: A restaurant on vicolo del Malpasso, with its own site at giulioterrinoni.it. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states the history of the business, so none is given here.

places.name: Al Pompiere

entries.name: Palazzo Farnese
entries.note: Commissioned in 1513 and finished in 1589 under Sangallo, Michelangelo, Vignola and Della Porta; entry is by guided tour booked through the palace's own site.

entries.name: Prospettiva del Borromini
entries.note: A colonnade 8.82 metres long built to read as about 35, with a 60-centimetre Roman warrior at the end that appears life-size from the entrance.

entries.name: Galleria Spada
entries.note: Four rooms hung as a seventeenth-century quadreria, frames touching and small pictures above large, as Federico Zeri arranged them in 1951; last admission 19.00, closed Tuesdays.

entries.name: Via Giulia
entries.note: Opened in 1508 and running 950 metres from piazza San Vincenzo Pallotti to piazza dell'Oro; its southern length lies in Regola and its northern length in Rione V Ponte.

entries.name: Via di Monserrato
entries.note: The spine of the rione's northern half, running into piazza Farnese and carrying the Spanish and English churches, Palazzo Incoronati and Chez Dédé.

entries.name: Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte
entries.note: A confraternity founded in 1538 to bury bodies recovered from the Tiber; its crypt took more than 8,000 and opens only by appointment with the Associazione Amici del Tevere.

entries.name: Sant'Eligio degli Orefici
entries.note: The goldsmiths asked Raphael in 1509 for a small temple; Roma Capitale gives access Monday to Friday 10.00 to 13.00 on prior booking.

entries.name: Carceri Nuove
entries.note: Innocent X's prison of 1652–1655 on via Giulia, offices towards the street and cells towards the Tiber; it held 600 men and 80 women in 1842.

entries.name: Fontana del Mascherone
entries.note: An antique mask pouring into an antique granite basin on via Giulia; Roma Capitale records that it ran wine for three days in 1720.

entries.name: Piazza Farnese
entries.note: Paved from 1545 and once used for tournaments, bullfights and summer floodings, with eight streets and alleys running into it.

entries.name: Roscioli Caffè Pasticceria
entries.note: A café on piazza Benedetto Cairoli, open 7.00 to 18.00 Monday to Saturday and 8.00 to 18.00 on Sunday, with a bookable indoor room.

entries.name: Al Pompiere
entries.note: A restaurant on the ground floor of Palazzo Cenci, on via di Santa Maria de' Calderari.

entries.name: Casa di Santa Brigida
entries.note: A guesthouse run by the Bridgettine sisters inside the Santa Brigida complex on piazza Farnese.

entries.name: Ponte Garibaldi
entries.note: Two segmental arches, 121 metres by 23; Roma Capitale states that the bridge joins the rione Regola to Trastevere.

links.note: Via Giulia's northern length lies in Rione V Ponte, which holds Palazzo Sacchetti, the Oratorio del Gonfalone and the Museo Criminologico.
Campo de' Fiori, the Giordano Bruno monument and the Arco degli Acetari are Parione's; Roma Capitale names Campo de' Fiori among Regola's limits.
